mcqs.question: Why can two instructions be in different pipeline stages during the same clock cycle?
options: Because the CPU runs at double its rated clock speed during those cycles
Because the compiler reorders instructions so they never depend on each other
Because each stage is built from separate hardware, so different stages can work on different instructions at once
Because one of the two instructions is always a no-op
mcqs.explanation: Pipelining works because fetch, decode, execute, etc. are physically separate hardware units. As long as two in-flight instructions occupy different stages, neither is idle. The clock speed doesn't change, and this has nothing to do with compiler reordering or inserted no-ops.

mcqs.question: A 5-stage pipeline is added to a CPU. What happens to a single instruction's own latency (fetch to write-back)?
options: It drops by roughly a factor of 5
It stays exactly the same, cycle for cycle
It becomes unmeasurable because instructions no longer complete individually
It stays about the same or increases slightly due to pipeline-register overhead
mcqs.explanation: Pipelining targets throughput, not the latency of one instruction. Splitting execution into stages adds pipeline-register delay between them, so a single instruction's total latency is the same or slightly worse than a non-pipelined design — the 5x gain shows up only in how many instructions finish per cycle once the pipeline is full.

mcqs.question: An N-stage pipeline rarely achieves its ideal N× speedup in practice. What is the primary reason?
options: Hazards (dependencies between instructions, branches) force stall cycles that leave stages idle
Clock speed must be reduced to support more stages
Modern compilers can't generate pipeline-friendly code
Cache misses make pipelining pointless
mcqs.explanation: Beyond the initial fill time, the main gap between ideal and real speedup is hazards — data, structural, and control dependencies that force bubbles into the pipeline. Compilers actually help pipelining via scheduling; clock speed is a separate design knob; cache misses are a real cost but not the reason pipeline speedup falls short of N×.

mcqs.question: A single instruction runs with nothing else in the pipeline (no other work queued). Does pipelining make it complete faster than a non-pipelined design?
options: Yes, always, by exactly the number of pipeline stages
No — pipelining doesn't reduce one instruction's own latency, and pipeline-register overhead can make it slightly slower
Yes, but only for load instructions
It depends on whether branch prediction is enabled
mcqs.explanation: Pipelining is a throughput technique: it overlaps independent instructions so more finish per second, but it does not shorten any single instruction's own stage-by-stage journey. With no other instructions to overlap with, a pipelined design offers no latency benefit and can be marginally slower due to added pipeline registers.

mcqs.question: Why don't real CPUs keep adding pipeline stages far beyond 20 to chase ever-higher clock speeds?
options: Compilers cannot generate code for pipelines deeper than 20 stages
Hardware physically cannot support more than 20 pipeline registers
Beyond a point, pipeline-register overhead and the growing cost of hazards/mispredictions outweigh the shrinking per-stage work
Deeper pipelines always have a lower CPI, so there is no trade-off to weigh
mcqs.explanation: Every added stage carries a fixed pipeline-register overhead and pushes hazard resolution further from fetch, so branch mispredictions and stalls get more expensive. Past a point, splitting work more finely barely shortens the clock period while flush penalties keep growing -- a real trade-off, not a hardware or compiler limit, and definitely not a free win for CPI.

mcqs.question: A 5-stage pipeline runs only 10 independent instructions. Why is its measured speedup (about 3.6x) noticeably below the ideal 5x?
options: The clock period increases when fewer instructions are run
Short instruction sequences always have more data hazards than long ones
5-stage pipelines only reach ideal speedup when running exactly 1000 instructions
The fixed 4-cycle fill overhead is a much larger fraction of the total when N is small
mcqs.explanation: Total cycles = N + (stages - 1); the '+4' fill overhead is constant regardless of N, so it dominates when N is small (10 + 4 = 14 vs an ideal 10) but becomes negligible when N is large (1000 + 4 vs 1000). It has nothing to do with hazard rates or a magic instruction count -- it's purely a fixed-cost-over-N effect.
